questions.question: How do the main axis and cross axis work in CSS Flexbox?
questions.title: Flexbox main axis and cross axis
questions.direct_answer: Flexbox lays out items along a main axis and aligns them along a perpendicular cross axis. flex-direction chooses the main axis and its direction; justify-content works on that main axis, while align-items works on the cross axis. The axes follow writing mode, so they should not be memorized only as horizontal and vertical.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner chooses Flexbox alignment properties from axes rather than memorized screen directions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating justify-content as horizontal and align-items as vertical in every flex direction.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention writing mode, auto margins, and the single-line boundary of align-content.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: flex-direction defines the main axis and item order direction.
justify-content distributes free space on the main axis.
align-items positions items on the cross axis.
Writing mode can change which physical direction an axis follows.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Flexbox container has two axes. The main axis is the direction in which flex items are laid out, and the cross axis runs perpendicular to it. flex-direction chooses row, row-reverse, column, or column-reverse, so the main axis is not permanently horizontal.

justify-content controls how remaining space is distributed along the main axis. Values such as flex-start, center, space-between, and space-evenly move or separate the group after the browser has worked out item sizes.

align-items controls each item's default alignment on the cross axis. For example, a row container can centre items vertically with align-items: center, while a column container uses the same declaration to centre them across the inline direction.

The axes follow the document's writing mode and direction. In a right-to-left row, main-start is on the right. That is why flex-start and flex-end are more accurate mental models than left and right.

For example, a toolbar can use display: flex, align-items: center, and gap for its controls, then margin-inline-start: auto on the account button to consume remaining main-axis space. A boundary is wrapped content: align-content affects space between multiple flex lines, but it has no effect on a single line. I also use gap for regular distance between flex items because it belongs to the container and does not require first-child or last-child margin exceptions. Spacing and alignment then remain separate decisions.

sections.title: Direction first, alignment second
sections.content: Before choosing an alignment property, determine flex-direction. That declaration establishes the main axis. Then use justify-content for that axis and align-items for the perpendicular axis. Logical start and end values make the same component work across writing directions.

sections.title: Free space is resolved after sizing
sections.content: Alignment does not replace item sizing. The browser first determines flex bases, distributes positive or negative free space, and then applies alignment to the remaining space. An item with auto margin on the main axis absorbs available space before justify-content can distribute it, which is useful for pushing one toolbar action away from the rest.

sections.title: Axes for the two common directions
sections.content:
flex-direction: row      main axis  ->   | cross axis down
flex-direction: column   main axis down   | cross axis ->
justify-content follows main; align-items follows cross

sections.title: Align a toolbar by axis
sections.content:
```html
<style>
  .toolbar { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.75rem; }
  .account { margin-inline-start: auto; }
</style>
<nav class="toolbar" aria-label="Editor">
  <button>Undo</button><button>Redo</button>
  <button class="account">Account</button>
</nav>
```
The buttons form a main-axis row, align-items centres their cross-axis boxes, and the auto margin consumes free space before Account.

questions.question: What do flex-grow, flex-shrink, and flex-basis control?
questions.title: flex-grow, flex-shrink, and flex-basis
questions.direct_answer: flex-basis supplies an item's starting main size, flex-grow controls how positive free space is shared, and flex-shrink controls how negative free space is removed. The browser resolves the basis first, then grows or shrinks eligible items. The flex shorthand is preferred because its values work as one sizing policy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands flex sizing as a free-space algorithm.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating grow factors as percentages or ignoring the automatic minimum size.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why shrink is base-size weighted and why the shorthand expresses a complete policy.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: flex-basis is the starting main size before free-space distribution.
flex-grow shares extra space using relative factors.
flex-shrink removes shortage and is weighted by the base size.
In browsers, flex: 1 commonly expands to flex: 1 1 0%, not simply width: 100%.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The three flex sizing properties describe one process. flex-basis provides the initial main size of an item before the container distributes free space. With flex-basis: auto, the browser considers the item's main-size property such as width and, if that is also auto, its content.

If the items use less room than the container provides, flex-grow decides which items may expand and in what ratio. grow values of 1 and 2 do not mean exact widths; they mean the second item receives twice the eligible positive free space.

If the items need more room than exists, flex-shrink controls contraction. Shrinking is weighted by both the shrink factor and the base size, which prevents a small item and a very large item from losing the same number of pixels by default.

For example, flex: 1 on three cards normally gives each a zero basis, lets each grow by the same factor, and permits shrinking. flex: 0 0 12rem creates a fixed 12rem main-size policy, while flex: none expands to 0 0 auto.

I prefer the flex shorthand because grow, shrink, and basis are designed to work together. A boundary is intrinsic minimum size: an item may still refuse to become narrower than its content until min-width: 0 or an appropriate wrapping rule allows it. Testing with unequal content is important because equal placeholder labels can hide the effects of auto bases and intrinsic minimums.

sections.title: Flexbox free-space distribution
sections.content: Use three plain questions: where does this item start, may it take surplus space, and may it give up space when the line is short? flex-basis, flex-grow, and flex-shrink answer those questions in that order.

sections.title: Ratios apply to free space
sections.content: Growth factors divide only the space left after bases and gaps, not the whole container. Shrink factors resolve negative free space and account for base sizes. Content constraints, minimum sizes, maximum sizes, and freezing during the flex algorithm can change the simple ratio, so computed dimensions are better evidence than assuming flex-grow is a percentage.

sections.title: Flex sizing sequence
sections.content:
1. Resolve each flex-basis
2. Compare total base sizes with container
3a. Space remains -> apply flex-grow
3b. Space is missing -> apply flex-shrink
4. Respect min/max size constraints

questions.question: What is the difference between justify-content, align-items, and align-content?
questions.title: Flexbox alignment properties compared
questions.direct_answer: justify-content distributes free space along the main axis, align-items sets the default cross-axis alignment of items within each flex line, and align-content distributes space between multiple flex lines. align-content needs wrapping, more than one line, and extra cross-axis space; otherwise it has no visible effect.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner distinguishes axis alignment from multi-line distribution.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using align-content on a single flex line and expecting it to centre items.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Check whether free space exists and mention align-self for one-item overrides.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: justify-content works along the current main axis.
align-items aligns items within each line on the cross axis.
align-content spaces multiple lines as a group.
align-self overrides align-items for one flex item.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
justify-content and the align properties answer different alignment questions. justify-content handles the main axis chosen by flex-direction and distributes leftover space around the items as a group.

align-items handles the cross axis inside each flex line. In a row, align-items: center centres items through the row's height. One item can override that shared value with align-self.

align-content does not align individual items. It distributes extra cross-axis space between flex lines, much like justify-content distributes main-axis space. It requires flex-wrap, at least two lines, and a container with more cross-size than those lines need.

For example, a wrapped tag list with a fixed min-height can use align-content: start so all lines remain grouped at the top, while align-items: center aligns each tag inside its own line.

A common boundary is a single-line toolbar: align-content will do nothing there. If centring fails, I confirm the flex direction, check which axis has free space, and choose the property for that axis instead of trying random alignment values.

sections.title: Align the group, the item, or the lines
sections.content: justify-content positions the item group on the main axis. align-items positions items within their current cross-axis line. align-content positions the collection of lines within the container. The number of lines and location of free space determine which property can produce a visible result.

sections.title: No free space means no distribution
sections.content: Distribution keywords need room to distribute. If the flex items already fill the main size, justify-content cannot move them. If one flex line stretches to the full cross size, align-content has no separate line group to place. Fixed item sizes, auto margins, stretching, and min/max constraints can consume free space before alignment runs.

sections.title: Choose the property by target
sections.content:
| Property | Axis | What moves | Multi-line required? |
|---|---|---|---|
| justify-content | Main | All items in a line | No |
| align-items | Cross | Items within each line | No |
| align-content | Cross | Flex lines as a group | Yes |

questions.question: When should you use Flexbox instead of CSS Grid?
questions.title: Choosing Flexbox or CSS Grid
questions.direct_answer: Use Flexbox when one row or one column should size and align itself mainly from its content, such as a toolbar or button group. Use Grid when rows and columns must coordinate as a two-dimensional layout, such as a dashboard. They are complementary: Grid can arrange regions while Flexbox aligns controls inside each region.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner chooses a layout model from the relationship among items.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using wrapped Flexbox when alignment must continue across rows.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how Grid, Flexbox, and normal flow can coexist at different component levels.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Flexbox is strongest for one-dimensional content flow.
Grid controls rows and columns together.
Choose from the relationship among items, not element count.
Nesting Grid and Flexbox is normal and useful.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Flexbox is usually the clearer choice when the layout problem is primarily one-dimensional. A navigation bar, toolbar, row of buttons, or vertically stacked card actions needs items to share and align space along one main axis, and the content often determines each item's size.

CSS Grid is stronger when both rows and columns must form a shared structure. A dashboard whose cards line up across columns and rows, or a page shell with named regions, benefits from explicit tracks rather than independent flex lines.

For example, I might use Grid for a product-card gallery so every card participates in the same responsive columns, then use Flexbox inside each card to keep its price and button aligned. The tools solve different levels of the layout.

The boundary is not simply one item versus many items, and Grid is not automatically less responsive. I look at whether alignment must continue across rows. Wrapped Flexbox lines are laid out independently, whereas Grid items share the grid tracks.

Normal document flow remains the simplest choice when neither axis needs special distribution. Adding a layout mode without a layout problem can make sizing harder to reason about.

sections.title: One axis or coordinated tracks
sections.content: Flexbox distributes content along one main axis and treats each wrapped line separately. Grid defines shared row and column tracks before placing items. The decision is about the relationship that must be preserved, not which feature is newer.

sections.title: Content-led and layout-led sizing
sections.content: Flexbox often begins with each item's content or flex basis, then shares free space. Grid often begins with track definitions and places items into those tracks, although intrinsic sizing is available in both. A component may use both modes at different nesting levels without conflict.

sections.title: Match the relationship
sections.content:
| Need | Better starting point |
|---|---|
| Align controls in one toolbar | Flexbox |
| Keep a gallery on shared columns | Grid |
| Let wrapped rows size independently | Flexbox |
| Align items across rows and columns | Grid |
| Ordinary reading flow | Normal flow |

``` Grid coordinates gallery columns; each card's Flexbox column pushes its action to the bottom.

questions.question: Why can a flex item overflow instead of shrinking?
questions.title: Flex item overflow and min-width
questions.direct_answer: A flex item can overflow because its default min-width is auto, which often preserves the item's min-content width. Long unbreakable text, a wide table, or nested content may therefore stop it from shrinking even when flex-shrink is 1. Set min-width: 0 on the shrinking item and give the content an appropriate wrapping or overflow rule.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can distinguish flex-shrink from intrinsic minimum sizing.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Increasing flex-shrink repeatedly while leaving min-width: auto in place.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the column equivalent min-height: 0 and choose content handling separately.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: flex-shrink does not override the automatic minimum size.
Long unbreakable content creates a large min-content width.
min-width: 0 lets a horizontal flex item shrink below that width.
Choose wrapping, clipping, or scrolling according to the content.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
flex-shrink: 1 permits an item to shrink during flex sizing, but it does not remove the item's minimum-size constraint. Flex items use an automatic minimum size, which commonly protects their min-content width.

If a child contains a long URL, a no-wrap label, a table, or another element with a large intrinsic width, that minimum can be wider than the available row. The item then overflows even though its shrink factor looks correct.

For example, in a sidebar-and-content layout, setting min-width: 0 on the content flex item allows it to become narrower than its longest unbroken text. overflow-wrap: anywhere can then break uncontrolled text, while an intentionally wide table may instead belong in a labelled horizontal scroller.

In a column flex container the equivalent problem can appear in the block direction, where min-height: 0 lets a scrolling child stay within the available height.

The boundary is content usability. min-width: 0 permits shrinking but does not decide how the content should respond. I still choose wrapping, ellipsis, or scrolling based on whether the full value must remain readable.

sections.title: Permission to shrink has two gates
sections.content: The shrink factor is one gate; the minimum size is another. An item can participate in negative free-space distribution and still stop at its min-content width. Removing the automatic minimum from the correct flex child lets the sizing algorithm continue.

sections.title: Fix the child that owns the constraint
sections.content: Apply min-width: 0 to the flex item whose contents refuse to fit, not indiscriminately to every ancestor. Then inspect the inner content. Text may need wrapping, media may need max-width: 100%, and data tables may need a contained scrollbar. This separates layout permission from content presentation.

sections.title: Why shrink stops
sections.content:
Negative free space -> flex-shrink allows reduction
                     -> auto min-width checks min-content
                     -> item stops and overflows
min-width: 0         -> item may continue shrinking

sections.title: Release the automatic minimum
